newsitem.title: GERMANY: Implications of enterprise value for German firms.
newsitem.headline: Implications of enterprise value for German firms.

text.p: By Guenter Dielmann, Senior Economist, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, Equity Research
The EV approach is growing in importance as a valuation measure for companies, sectors and the equity markets as a whole.

We have been using this method now for over a year. While we have outlined the broad principles of the concept we have not yet discussed the methodology in detail, which was due to the time and problems involved in installing the number-crunching systems, finding the right model and obtaining reliable results. Meanwhile we feel comfortable with our figures which allow for the special features of German accounting regulations.

Enterprise value represents the value of a company as a whole for all its capital providers (in other words both lenders and equity investors). Broadly speaking, total enterprise value is calculated from a company's market capitalisation - the value of shareholders' equity - and debt. It therefore takes no account of a company's capital structure.

The EV approach builds on the basic theory developed by Miller and Modigliani ("Divisional Policy, Growth and Valuation", Journal of Business, 1961) that a company's value is not affected by changes in its capital structure (e.g. by a capital increase; this statement is only valid to a certain extent in countries like the US where earnings distributed to shareholders are taxed twice while the interest paid to lenders of capital is taxed only once).

Share buybacks, for instance, do not affect enterprise value as assets are merely switched and, in theory, do not increase a company's market capitalisation. In practice, though, market capitalisation does rise because investors assume the company will use its remaining funds more efficiently and increase its return on capital employed.

A simple example can be used to illustrate how different capital structures affect valuations. Companies A and B are essentially identical except for their indebtedness. According to Miller and Modigliani, Company B's market capitalisation must be 25 units higher than Company A's if Company A's net debt is 25 units higher than Company B's.
Company A Company B
Sales 100 100
EBIT* 5 5
Net interest result (1.5) 0.3
Pretax result 3.5 5.3
Reported net profit 1.75 2.65
Market capitalisation 25 50
Net debt 20 (5)
EV/EBIT 9 9
* earnings before interest income and taxes

In P/E terms Company A's rating is a good deal lower than company B's. On a EV basis the two companies have the same valuation. In theory, Company B could borrow funds and invest them in new projects or capacity expansion. If the project's rate of return exceeds its cost of capital, this should come to be reflected in the company's share price. Owing to its debt situation Company A only has this option to a limited extent. Why are we focusing more on EV?

- The quality of comparative sector and company valuations can be substantially enhanced, both at the international and the national level, if suitable measures are applied, such as adjusted EBIT and EBDIT (pretax DVFA/SG adjustments and adjustments for the change in pension provisions) and adjustment cash flow figures. The EV/EBDIT measure is not affected by differences in tax rates, capital structure or depreciation policy. Structural differences, for instance in the local taxation systems, are eliminated.

- EV reveals the relatively high indebtedness of most cyclical companies and puts their P/Es, which are generally comparatively low, into perspective. Companies in "old" industries have accumulated very high pension obligations, which are also reflected in EV and the valuation multiples.
- EV is a much better indication of a company's potential acquisition price since the buyer also takes over the company's debt.

- The EV approach makes it possible to calculate other ratios covering the enterprise as a whole, like EV/sales or EV/capital employed. The sales-to-market- capitalisation ratio, for instance, compares the company's consolidated sales with the market value of its equity. This excluded minority interests, while the sales figure is not adjusted for the sales theoretically attributable to minority holdings.
(The author is senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Equity Research in Frankfurt. The views expressed are those of the author alone and not of Reuters.)
